title: Early V2 signal concentration depended on time window and unit scaling in public macaque texture responses
abstract: We tested whether response timing changes a prior null result for V1-to-V2 spectral compression. We used 205 neurons, 135 images and 20 repeats in the Freeman/Ziemba Brain-Score public split. We measured cross-validated spectra in 60 ms windows with 200 paired draws of 50 neurons per area. For texture responses at 40-100 ms, standardized V2 top-five signal share exceeded V1 by 0.116 (conditional draw interval 0.028 to 0.204). At 140-200 ms the difference was 0.007 (-0.055 to 0.069). The late-minus-early exponent change was -0.488 (-0.900 to -0.076), but raw-count and fixed-scale exponent intervals included zero. Comparing V1 at 40-100 ms with V2 at 60-120 ms gave near-zero standardized differences in both metrics. An exploratory population onset check found only a 2-3 ms area difference, which weakens a simple 20 ms delay account. The long-window null therefore does not describe every response phase, but the early concentration increase is sensitive to timing and unit scale. Limits include one public split, no animal-level intervals, fixed images, and finite-noise PCA axes. This does not explain mouse compression or establish a species difference. Original code, aggregate evidence and a pinned external-data recipe support reproduction.
